item.title: Hear whether a reviewer should accept an analogy
item.summary: A critic assesses a transport analogy for the operation of a library.
item.transcript_text:
Reviewer: Calling the loans desk a railway platform is appealing. Both have peaks, and there are places where people can jam. The analogy helps you ask where a queue should form.
Author: Can I use it to organise the whole article?
Reviewer: A passenger usually knows where they’re going before reaching the platform. A library visitor can arrive with a question and discover a different task in conversation. At the reference desk, that exchange isn't necessarily a delay to remove.
Author: Should I drop the queue figures?
Reviewer: Keep them for circulation. Let the reference desk show where the comparison stops working.
Author: I can show how the same minute can be congestion in one place and the service itself in another.

questions.prompt: Where does the reviewer find the analogy useful?
options: For every reason people enter a library
For selecting books on behalf of others
For movement through a process with a defined purpose
For training railway ticket staff
questions.explanation: The analogy helps identify bottlenecks where movements are reasonably predictable.

questions.prompt: What limits the analogy at the reference desk?
options: Every conversation has a fixed endpoint
A visitor’s task can change during the interaction
Library staff refuse to measure time
The desk cannot attract a queue
questions.explanation: The reference encounter may help the visitor discover what they need.

questions.prompt: What should happen to queue figures?
options: Keep them, but limit their role in the argument
Discard them because they never show anything useful
Use them as the only test of conversation quality
Replace them with railway ticket figures
questions.explanation: The reviewer applies the measures where their interpretation holds.

questions.prompt: What is the author’s proposed framing?
options: All longer encounters improve service
Railway passengers always wait longer
The point of reference work is to shorten every interaction
The same time can be unproductive delay or a useful part of service
questions.explanation: The last line distinguishes congestion from the work a service provides.

questions.prompt: What wider reviewing principle is illustrated?
options: Use a familiar comparison for every part of a subject
Reject analogies in any article with measurements
State what an analogy illuminates and where it ceases to help
Choose comparisons based solely on average time
questions.explanation: The reviewer wants a limited analogy with its boundary made clear.
